title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code
summary: The source generator now marks every formatter and resolver it emits with `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]`, so coverage tools skip them. The attribute sits inside `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. The AI edited the 6 code templates and one helper, TransformUtilities.cs. It re-recorded 222 test snapshots (saved copies of the expected generator output) and added a test file and a README note.
head: a0aa5ab2

claims.claim: 220 of the 222 changed snapshot files only gain the attribute and its #if/#endif lines. The other 2 are both in Resources/GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember/: in Named a brace moves to its own line, and in Ordinal there is one extra blank line.
claims.why_this_tier: This is a count from a script that sorts the diff. It describes the change; it does not by itself show the snapshots are correct.

claims.claim: All 222 changed snapshots are exactly what the new generator emits, and that code compiles. The snapshot tests pass 169 of 169 after the change (167 of 167 before).
claims.why_this_tier: The snapshot tests run the real generator, compare its output with the committed files, then compile it. They pass.

claims.claim: The 6 committed template .cs files emit the same text as their edited .tt sources. Regenerating with dotnet-t4 matches 6 of 6 after the change. The same method matches 6 of 6 unchanged templates before the change. As a control, the new output differs from the old .cs files in 6 of 6, so the comparison does catch changes.
claims.why_this_tier: We regenerated the real templates and compared the text they emit, ignoring layout, after checking the method on the old code. It is not a byte-for-byte match with Visual Studio's tool.

claims.claim: Every generated file has the attribute, and every copy sits inside the #if guard. This holds for a sample with an integer-keyed object, a string-keyed object, an enum, a union and a resolver.
claims.why_this_tier: The 2 new CodeCoverageExclusionTests fail before the change (2 of 2) and pass after.

chain.link: The new tests fail before the change.
The new tests pass after the change.

claims.claim: The TransformUtilities.cs edit is needed. Without it, a formatter inside a generic type with constraints comes out as `{#if ...` on one line, and the generated code fails to compile (CS1040).
claims.why_this_tier: Undoing only that line makes GenerationTests.GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember fail (168 of 169 pass); restoring it makes it pass. A manual run shows the failure is compile error CS1040.

chain.link: With the edit undone, the snapshot test fails (scripted run).
The failure is error CS1040 in the generated code (manual run).

claims.claim: The TransformUtilities.cs edit has one visible side effect in the snapshots: an extra blank line in the Ordinal formatter of GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember.
claims.why_this_tier: The diff-sorting script counted it, and the run with the edit removed confirmed it. Two things are not machine-checked: that the blank line is harmless, and that EnumTemplate gets the same blank line, which we found by reading the code.

claims.claim: The change breaks the build for users who already put [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their resolver by hand: they get compile error CS0579. The generator now adds the attribute to the user's own partial resolver classes (ResolverTemplate, CompositeResolverTemplate). The user picks their visibility, and they can be public.
claims.why_this_tier: It changes public API, so a person must decide. The attribute ends up in the user's public type and breaks the build for a plausible existing pattern. An experiment on the real generator confirms this: it builds before the change and fails after.
claims.owner_role: MessagePack-CSharp maintainer who owns public API and breaking changes

claims.claim: The AI says the guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` is needed because the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework.
claims.why_this_tier: Only the AI's word backs this, and our check contradicts it. The attribute is in the netstandard2.0 and net472 reference assemblies, and code without the guard compiles on both. So the guard turns the feature off on 2 targets. Whether to turn it on there is a product decision.

claims.claim: The README says all generated formatters and resolvers carry [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage], but only where it is available: not on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework.
claims.why_this_tier: Documentation is not machine-checked. Its first sentence matches C-2297-04. Its second repeats the claim that the attribute is unavailable, which our check contradicts (C-2297-08).

claims.claim: The snapshot check is sensitive to line endings. It passes here because .gitattributes checks out the 225 snapshot .cs files with Windows line endings (CRLF). With Unix line endings (LF), 89 of 169 tests fail.
claims.why_this_tier: A count from running the tests on a copy with the snapshots converted to LF. It adds a condition to C-2297-02; it does not back a change.

found: The diff classifier (script) flagged 2 of 222 snapshots that change beyond attribute and guard lines, both in Resources/GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember/: Named (the line `{\tinternal sealed class ...` is split so `{` stands alone) and Ordinal (one added blank line).

The TransformUtilities.cs edit has no stated reason (the commit message has no body). We found it is required: with it reverted, the generated code fails with CS1040; its one visible side effect is the extra blank line in the Ordinal snapshot.

We found the guard too strict: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in the netstandard2.0 and net472 reference assemblies, so netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers silently get no exclusion. The README and the test comment state the opposite.

We found a break for existing users: a hand-written [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on the user's partial resolver compiles on base and fails with CS0579 (duplicate attribute) on the branch. No branch test covers it.
CodeCoverageExclusionTests hard-codes the guard text, so widening the guard also means changing the test.
By reading the test verifier: no preprocessor symbols are set in the snapshot compilations, so the guarded-out path (netstandard2.0, .NET Framework) is never compiled by the tests.

The diff classifier (script) flagged 1 Resources directory with no test method (Resources/InterfaceUnion/, 3 files). It already exists on base, is not run by any test, and the branch leaves it without the attribute, so it is now stale.
Correction to the handoff: the verifier writes actual output to Resources/ only when WRITE_EXPECTED is defined (the method is [Conditional("WRITE_EXPECTED")]); a plain test run only compares.
When generated content differs, the test framework reports 'Expected source file list to match' rather than the content diff, which hides the real cause (here CS1040).

refused.what: [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] added to the user-declared partial resolver classes (C-2297-07)
refused.why: It changes the consumer's public type metadata and breaks the build (CS0579) for users who already excluded their resolver by hand. That is a public API and compatibility call, so the owner decides.

scope_drift: None found. The TransformUtilities.cs edit looked like drift (it has no stated reason) but the removal test shows the feature does not compile without it.
not_checked: The text of issue #2297: we could not read it here, so R-2297-1..4 are inferred from the branch title and commit.
macOS: all runs were on Linux (6.18.44, x86_64). Per .gitattributes the snapshots check out as CRLF on every OS, but that was not run on a Mac.
Compiling real generated output for netstandard2.0, netstandard2.1 or net472 consumers: only a small probe was compiled for those targets.
Whether coverage tools (coverlet, dotnet-coverage) actually drop the generated types from their reports.
Unity, Mono and other builds with their own preprocessor symbols; netstandard1.x and .NET Framework before 4.0.
Union and enum formatters nested in a generic type with constraints: no snapshot covers them; the need for the edit (Union) and the blank line (Enum) are by reading only.
Byte-for-byte equality with Visual Studio's TextTemplatingFilePreprocessor: dotnet-t4 was compared on emitted text only.
